questions.question: Which is not included in the FAB classification of acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) L3 subtype?

options.A: Presence of lymphoblasts with vacuoles and cytoplasmic blebs

explanation.text: Unlike Burkitt lymphoma cells, which typically express surface immunoglobulins, the lymphoblasts in ALL L3 subtype do not express surface immunoglobulins. Instead, they express other markers, such as CD10 and CD19.

FAB classification of ALL: L1 L2 L3 Occurrence More common - Less common Morphology Small homogenous blasts Large heterogenous blasts Large homogenous blasts Cytoplasm Scant blue Moderately weak basophilic Abundant basophilic with prominent vacuoles Nucleus Regular Irregular nuclear outlines - Nucleoli Small & indistinct Prominent - Chromatin Coarse & dark purple Pink - Prognosis Best - Poor ALL-L3 is similar to Burkitt’s lymphoma.
The image below shows the FAB types of ALL.
Presence of lymphoblasts with vacuoles and cytoplasmic blebs ( Option A): The presence of lymphoblasts with vacuoles and cytoplasmic blebs is a characteristic feature of L3 subtype ALL.

Association with Epstein-Barr virus ( Option C): Burkitt lymphoma is strongly associated with Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) infection. However, while EBV infection may be present in some ALL cases, it is not a defining characteristic of the ALL L3 subtype. t(9;22) Philadelphia chromosome ( Option D): The Philadelphia chromosome, resulting from the translocation t(9;22), is associated with a different subtype of ALL (Philadelphia chromosome-positive ALL, or Ph+ ALL) rather than the L3 subtype. Ph+ ALL is characterised by the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene (190 kDa fusion protein).

questions.question: Which of the following is not associated with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) regarding chromosomes?

explanation.text: t(15;17) translocation is not associated with ALL; rather, it is seen in acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APML), a type of acute myeloid leukaemia, where t(15;17) translocation leads to the formation of a PML-RARα fusion protein (Option D).

Genetic abnormalities associated with ALL: B-cell ALL with recurrent cytogenetic abnormalities: t(12;21): ETV6-RUNX1 (25% of the cases) (Option B ruled out). t(v,11) (KMT2A-MLL). t(9;22): BCR-ABL1 (Option A ruled out). It produces a 190 kDa fusion protein. t(5;14): IgH-IL3. B-cell ALL with hyperdiploidy. B-cell ALL with hypodiploidy. B-cell ALL t(1;19): TCF3-PBX1. (Option C ruled out).
BCR-ABL1 like ALL (provisional entity in 2018 WHO). iAMP 21 ALL. T-cell ALL: NOTCH1 mutations are most common (50-70% of the cases).

questions.question: A 4-year-old male presents with fever, bleeding gums, and fatigue for 5 days. CBC shows Hb of 8g%, TLC 30,000/µL, and platelet count of 40,000/µL. A differential count shows an increased number of immature white blood cells. A bone marrow aspiration is done, as shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.text: The clinical presentation of fatigue, fever, and bleeding gums, along with anaemia, thrombocytopenia, leukocytosis with a high proportion of immature white blood cells, and bone marrow aspirate showing lymphoblasts (numerous large cells with a high nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio, round to oval nuclei, fine, dispersed chromatin pattern with scant, basophilic cytoplasm ) is indicative of acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL).

Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia: Neoplasms of immature B (pre-B) or T (pre-T) cells (known as lymphoblasts). It is the most common cancer among children. Peak incidence: 3 rd year. Clinical features: Abrupt stormy onset. Symptoms Due to decline in normal marrow function. Fatigue - anaemia. Infections - neutropenia. Bleeding - thrombocytopenia Mass effects Bone pain due to marrow expansion and infiltration of the subperiosteum.

Generalised lymphadenopathy. Hepatosplenomegaly. Testicular enlargement. Mediastinal mass in T-ALL (Superior mediastinal syndrome). CNS manifestations Headache. Vomiting. Nerve palsies. Morphology: Hypercellular bone marrow. Lymphoblasts have more condensed chromatin, less conspicuous nucleoli, and scanty agranular cytoplasm than myeloblasts. Cytochemistry: Myeloperoxidase (MPO) negative, sudan black negative.
Note: Myeloblasts are large cells with scanty blue cytoplasm, round, oval or irregular nuclei, fine chromatin, and multiple prominent nucleoli.

questions.question: Which of the following markers will be negative on immunophenotyping of a patient with early pre-B acute leukaemia?

explanation.text: CD10 and Cytoplasmic immunoglobulins (Cy Ig) are negative in early pre-B acute leukaemia but become positive in pre-B ALL. Immunophenotyping of Acute Lymphocytic Leukemia (ALL): Type of ALL Immunophenotype Early Pre-B ALL TdT, DR, CD19, CD24 Pre-B ALL TdT, DR, CD10, CD19, CD20, CD24, Cy Ig Common ALL CD19+, CD10+/CALLA+ Mature B ALL DR, CD19 CD20, CD24, Surface Ig Pro-T ALL CD3, CD7 Pre-T ALL TdT, CD2, CD3, CD4, CD5, CD7, CD8, CD34 Mature T ALL CD2, CD7, TdT

questions.question: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding the prognosis of ALL? Adults have a worse prognosis as compared to children aged 2-9 years. White females have a good survival rate as compared to black males. The Philadelphia chromosome (t(9;22)) is associated with a favourable prognosis. Higher white blood cell counts at diagnosis are associated with a better prognosis. Hypodiploidy in B-ALL is associated with a better prognosis.

explanation.text: Prognostic factors associated with ALL: Determinants Favourable Unfavourable WBC/µL <10,000 >1,00,000 (Statement D) Age 2-9 years <1 year, >10 years (Statement A) Gender Female Male Ethnicity White (Statement B) Black Lymph node, liver, spleen enlargement Absent Present Testicular enlargement Absent Present CNS involvement Absent Present FAB morphologic features L1, early pre-B cell ALL L3, Pre-B cell & mature B-cell ALL Ploidy Hyperdiploidy Hypodiploidy (Statement E) Cytogenetic markers Trisomy 4, 10, 17, t(12;21) t(9;22), t(4;11) (Statement C) Remission states <14 days >14 days

questions.question: A 7-year-old boy presents with fever, fatigue, and bone pain. On physical examination, there is notable hepatosplenomegaly and testicular enlargement. Laboratory findings show elevated white blood cell count and blasts on peripheral smear. Immunophenotyping reveals the presence of markers CD3, CD5, and CD10. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.text: This young boy with elevated WBC counts and blast cells on a peripheral smear, combined with testicular involvement and positive CD3, CD5, and CD10, is most likely to have T-cell acute lymphocytic leukaemia (ALL).

Important features of different types of leukaemia: ALL AML (Option A) CML (Option D) B cell -ALL (Option C) T cell -ALL (Option B) Most common Less common (15%) M2 (M/C) - Age Children Teenagers Adults (15-40 years) Middle-Elderly Mutation Loss of function PAX5, E2A, EBF Gain of function NOTCH1 t(15:17) in M3, t (8:21) in M2 t(9:22) BCR-ABL fusion gene.

Prognosis Good Poor Good Good Organ Involvement No tissue involvement CNS, Mediastinum, Testes, Bone pain Hepatosplenomegaly, gum hyperplasia, chloroma Massive splenomegaly, hepatomegaly Stain PAS+ Acid Phosphatase MPO+, NSE + Decreased NAP/LAP score Markers CD 19,20,21 CD 1,2, 3, 5,7, 10 (CALLA antigen) CD 13, 33, and 117 CD 25

questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding the M4 subtype of AML based on FAB classification is true?

options.A: It is associated with t(8:21), called AML with maturation.
options.B: It is associated with t(15:17), called acute promyelocytic leukaemia
options.C: It is associated with CBF-MYH fusion, called acute myelomonocytic leukaemia
options.D: It is associated with MPO positivity, called AML without maturation.

explanation.text: Acute myelocytic leukemia (M4) type, also called acute myelomonocytic leukaemia, is associated with the CBF-MYH fusion gene. FAB classification of AML Subtype Name Features AML-M0 AML undifferentiated MPO negative AML-M1 AML without maturation (Option D) MPO + AML-M2 AML with maturation (Option A) Most common t(8:21) RUNX1-RUNX1T1 fusion Associated with chloroma.

**AML-M3 Acute promyelocytic leukaemia (Option B):** t(15:17) - PML-RARα fusion Blocks promyelocyte → myelocyte transformation Bone marrow: Auer rods form criss-cross called faggot cell Can cause DIC PAS+ AML-M4 Acute myelomonocytic leukaemia (Option C) Associated with inv 16 and CBF-MYH fusion gene Gums - gum hypertrophy Skin - leukaemia cutis MPO+, NSE + AML-M5 Acute monocytic leukaemia Gums - gum hypertrophy Skin - leukaemia cutis MPO-, NSE + AML-M6 Acute erythroid leukaemia Also called DI Guglielmo Disease Diffuse PAS+, CD71 AML-M7 Acute megakaryocytic leukaemia Bone Marrow aspiration gives a dry tap PAS+, CD41 and CD61

questions.question: A 12-year-old boy presents with fatigue, bruising, and intermittent fevers for the past few weeks. Physical examination reveals the following findings. Immunophenotyping of the biopsy specimen shows CD43 and MPO positivity. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.text: This young child with nonspecific systemic symptoms, MPO positivity, and an image showing orbital swelling and proptosis suggests chloroma associated with AML with maturation (AML-M2). Chloroma: A.k.a Myeloblastoma/Granulocytic Sarcoma. It is not a benign tumour, but it has a greenish colour. Site: Soft tissue involvement in orbit leads to proptosis. Associated with AML M2 and M5. Peripheral smear findings: Myeloblasts.
Arbiskov cells: Atypical monocytes/macrophages. Markers: MPO (green colour), CD 43, CD 45 and Lysozyme.
**Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) (Option A):** ALL mostly stains PAS and Acid phosphatase and are negative for CD43 and MPO.
**Acute promyelocytic leukaemia (Option C):** The M3 subtype of Acute Myeloid Leukaemia (AML) is associated with disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) and PAS positivity.
**Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma (Option D):** Burkitt's lymphoma (non-Hodgkin lymphoma), is characterised by cervical lymphadenopathy, causes jaw swelling and CD19, 20, and PAX5 positivity.

questions.question: A 28-year-old female was admitted to the hospital with complaints of frequent nosebleeds, reports of sudden onset chest pain and dyspnea. On examination, she has petechiae and ecchymoses on her skin. Laboratory tests revealed WBC 15,000/µL, haemoglobin 8 g/dL, platelets 20,000/µL and elevated prothrombin time. A peripheral blood smear shows the following findings. Further testing confirms which of the following associated conditions?

explanation.text: This patient's history of sudden onset symptoms with pancytopenia, high prothrombin time, and Auer-rods on blood smear suggests disseminated intravascular coagulation secondary to acute promyelocytic leukaemia associated with t(15:17) translocation. M3 AML/ Acute promyelocytic leukemia: Genetics: t(15:17) translocation causes PML-RARA (retinoic acid receptor alpha) fusion protein formation. Blocks promyelocyte → myelocyte maturation.

Diagnosis of choice: FISH Smear findings: Increased promyelocytes. Auer Rods: Fused granules in promyelocytes Faggot Cells: Auer rods with a crisscross pattern. Laboratory: Low hemoglobin and platelets. > 20% blasts on peripheral and bone marrow smear Stain: PAS + CD markers: CD 13, 33 + Complication: Disseminated intravascular coagulation therefore, chemotherapy is not recommended.

Treatment: ATRA (All-trans-retinoic-acid) + As 2 O 3 (arsenic trioxide) Best prognosis among all AML. t(12:21) translocation (Option A) is seen in ALL and has a good prognosis. They are negative for auer rods. t(9:22) translocation (Option C): Philadelphia chromosome associated with CML and ALL (worse prognosis). CML: t(9;22) results in a BCR-ABL fusion protein of 210 kDa. ALL: t(9;22) results in a BCR-ABL fusion protein of 190 kDa.

Presents with massive hepatosplenomegaly. Labs show normal RBC with elevated TLC (>40,000) and platelet counts. Peripheral smear reveals immature WBC with basophils called bone marrow appearance. t(8:21) translocation (Option D): t(8:21) translocation is seen in the M2 subtype of AML (most common). Associated with chloroma. The smear reveals > 10% mature myeloid cells, not Auer rods.

questions.question: Which of the following types of AML, according to the FAB classification, is associated with Down’s syndrome?

explanation.text: Acute megakaryoblastic leukaemia (AML M7) is notably associated with Down's syndrome. Acute megakaryocytic leukaemia: Least common type of AML. The megakaryocytes release platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF), causing myelofibrosis. It is the most common AML in Down’s syndrome and the most common type of leukemia in Down's syndrome is ALL. Antibodies against megakaryocyte-specific markers (GPIIb/IIIa or vWF) can be seen.
Bone marrow aspiration yields a ‘dry tap’ due to fibrosis in the bone marrow.

questions.question: Which of the following is associated with a good prognosis according to WHO classification of AML?

explanation.text: AML defined by specific genetic abnormalities are associated with a good prognosis due to the presence of targetable mutations and the availability of specific therapies, such as ATRA for APL. Examples include: t(8;21) (RUNX1-RUNX1T1) inv(16) CBFB-MYH11 t(15;17) PML-RARA WHO Classification of AML: AML with Recurrent Genetic Abnormalities (good prognosis): t(8;21)(q22;q22.1); RUNX1-RUNX1T1 inv(16) (CBFB-MYH11) t(15;17)(q24.1;q21.1); PML-RARA. t(1;22) AML with Myelodysplasia-Related Changes (bad prognosis) Therapy-Related Myeloid Neoplasms (bad prognosis) AML, Not Otherwise Specified (NOS) (bad prognosis) AML with minimal differentiation AML without maturation AML with myelocytic maturation AML with myelomonocytic maturation.
AML with monocytic maturation. AML with erythroid maturation. AML with megakaryocytic maturation. AML associated with Down's syndrome - AMLM7.

questions.question: What is the most likely immunophenotype associated with the condition indicated by the peripheral blood smear shown below?

explanation.text: The peripheral smear shows myeloblasts (large, irregularly shaped cells with prominent nuclei and moderately granular cytoplasm), and needle-like inclusions in the cytoplasm of blasts (Auer rods), suggesting acute myeloid leukaemia (AML). The immunophenotype associated with AML is CD13+, CD33+, CD34+, and HLA-DR+. AML is characterised by the presence of myeloid lineage markers. CD13, CD33, and CD34 are commonly expressed on AML blasts.
Additionally, the presence of HLA-DR is typical in AML immunophenotyping.

**CD19+, CD20-, CD22+, CD79a- (Option B):** This immunophenotyping pattern is characteristic of B-cell ALL. In B-ALL, blasts typically express B-cell markers such as CD19, CD22, and CD79a. CD20 expression is variable but often negative in B-ALL.

**CD3+, CD4+, CD8+, CD5- (Option C):** This immunophenotyping pattern is indicative of T-cell ALL. In T-ALL, blasts express T-cell markers such as CD3, CD4, CD8, and CD5, reflecting their origin from T-cell precursors.

**CD10+, CD19+, CD20+, CD22- (Option D):** This immunophenotyping pattern is suggestive of B-cell Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (B-CLL). In B-CLL, leukemic cells express B-cell markers such as CD19, CD20, and CD22. CD10 expression is variable but often present in B-CLL cases.

questions.question: A 55-year-old female presented with fatigue, easy bruising, and recurrent infections over the past few months. On examination, there is mild splenomegaly, but no lymphadenopathy is noted. Laboratory tests reveal pancytopenia. A peripheral blood smear shows normocytic normochromic red blood cells and no blast cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.text: In this scenario, the patient presents with pancytopenia, fatigue, easy bruising, and recurrent infections. The absence of blast cells in the peripheral smear despite the presence of cytopenias suggests aleukemic leukaemia. Aleukemic leukaemia or aleukemic leukaemia cutis is leukaemia without circulating blast cells in the peripheral blood. While blast cells may be absent in the peripheral smear, they can still be present in the bone marrow.

The malignant white cells invade the skin before they appear in the peripheral blood or bone marrow. Patients may present with symptoms similar to other types of leukaemia, including fatigue, weakness, fever, weight loss, and easy bruising or bleeding. Diagnosis requires a high index of suspicion, as the absence of blast cells in the peripheral blood smear can make it challenging to identify.
A bone marrow biopsy may reveal the presence of leukaemia cells, aiding in diagnosis.

**Aplastic anemia (Option A):** Aplastic anaemia is characterised by pancytopenia (low red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets) due to bone marrow failure. Unlike leukaemia, it does not involve the overproduction of immature cells (blast cells) and does not typically present with blasts on peripheral smears.

**Myelodysplasia (Option B):** Myelodysplasia, or myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS), is a group of blood disorders characterised by abnormal development and function of blood-forming cells in the bone marrow. In MDS, the bone marrow produces immature or defective blood cells that may not function properly.

**Myeloproliferative disorder (Option D):** Myeloproliferative disorders (MPDs) are a group of conditions characterised by excessive production of mature blood cells. Unlike leukaemia, MPDs do not typically present with pancytopenia (reduced levels of all blood cell types) and do not involve the overproduction of blast cells seen in leukaemia.

questions.question: A 45-year-old female presents with complaints of occasional headaches and blurred vision. Laboratory tests reveal isolated thrombocytosis without significant leukocytosis or erythrocytosis. Bone marrow biopsy shows increased megakaryocytes. Which of the following types of myeloproliferative neoplasm (MPN) is most likely to be diagnosed based on these findings?

explanation.text: Essential thrombocytosis is a type of myeloproliferative neoplasm which is characterized by isolated thrombocytosis without any without significant leukocytosis or erythrocytosis, along with increased megakaryocytes in bone marrow biopsy It is asymptomatic in more than half of the cases and is usually diagnosed incidentally Less than 50% patients have symptoms related to thrombosis or hemorrhage Symptoms include Bleeding tendency Microvascular occlusion Thrombosis of major arteries (leading to CVA and transient ischemic attacks), and vasomotor symptoms such as headache, visual disturbances, and syncope.

Mild splenomegaly and rarely hepatomegaly and lymphadenopathy Diagnosis Criteria for Early/Prefibrotic ET Sustained platelet count ≥ 450 x 10^9/L Megakaryocyte proliferation Absence of criteria for other myeloid neoplasms Absence of JAK2, CALR, or MPL mutation Polycythemia Vera (PV) (Option A): It is characterized by increased red blood cell mass, leading to erythrocytosis.

Associated with JAK2 mutation Symptoms: headaches, dizziness, and pruritus due to hyperviscosity. Laboratory findings typically include elevated hemoglobin and hematocrit levels, leukocytosis, and thrombocytosis.

**Bone marrow biopsy shows hypercellularity with increased erythropoiesis Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (Option C):** CML is characterized by the Philadelphia chromosome (BCR-ABL fusion gene). Patients present with leukocytosis, predominantly neutrophils, and may have splenomegaly. Laboratory findings- elevated white blood cell count, left-shifted granulocytes, and basophilia. Treatment often involves tyrosine kinase inhibitors targeting the BCR-ABL fusion protein.

**Primary Myelofibrosis (PMF) (Option D):** It is characterized by bone marrow fibrosis, leading to cytopenias and splenomegaly. Symptoms- fatigue, weight loss, and abdominal discomfort due to splenomegaly. Laboratory findings: anemia, leukoerythroblastosis, and teardrop-shaped red blood cells (dacrocytes) on peripheral smears. JAK2 mutation is commonly found in PMF Bone marrow biopsy shows fibrosis with increased megakaryocytes.

questions.question: A 50-year-old male presents with complaints of headaches, dizziness, and pruritus. Physical examination reveals a plethora and splenomegaly. Laboratory tests show elevated hemoglobin and hematocrit levels. Which of the following criteria are consistent with the Polycythemia Vera (PV) diagnosis?

options.D: Presence of CALR or MPL mutation

explanation.text: Diagnostic Criteria of Polycythemia Vera: Major criteria: Hb: > 16.5 g/dL in men and 16 g/dL in women. Hct: > 49% in men and > 48% in women. BM Trilineage myeloproliferative with pleomorphic megakaryocytes. Presence of JAK2 mutation. Minor Criteria: Subnormal serum erythropoietin level. Clinical features: Increased Hb causes stasis and neurological abnormalities. Increased TLC causes itching after a hot water bath and flushing.
A high platelet count causes bleeding tendencies. Hepatosplenomegaly.

**Sustained platelet count ≥ 450 x 10^9/L (Option A):** This criterion is not indicative of polycythemia vera (PV). Instead, it is a characteristic of Essential Thrombocytosis (ET), which is characterized by isolated thrombocytosis without significant erythrocytosis or leukocytosis.

**Presence of JAK2 mutation (Option C):** While the presence of JAK2 mutation is a major diagnostic criterion for PV, it is not the only criterion. The presence of JAK2 mutations may also be observed in other myeloproliferative neoplasms like Essential Thrombocythemia (ET) or Primary Myelofibrosis (PMF).

**Presence of CALR or MPL mutation (Option D):** CALR and MPL mutations are typically associated with other myeloproliferative neoplasms, such as Essential Thrombocythemia (ET) or Primary Myelofibrosis (PMF), and are not specific to Polycythemia Vera (PV).

questions.question: A 55-year-old female presents to the clinic with complaints of frequent headaches, dizziness, and occasional burning pain in her hands and feet. Examination reveals splenomegaly. Her complete blood count shows a platelet count of 12,00,000/µL. The peripheral blood smear shows marked thrombocytosis with giant platelets. Which of the following is not true regarding this condition?

options.A: Characterized by the presence of megakaryocytic hyperplasia.
options.B: Associated with JAK2, CALR, or MPL mutations.
options.C: Bone marrow biopsy typically shows increased reticulin fibrosis.
options.D: Increased risk of thrombotic and hemorrhagic events.

explanation.text: The clinical presentation is consistent with Essential Thrombocytosis, which typically does not show a significant increase in reticulin fibers in the bone marrow at diagnosis. Increased reticulin fibrosis is more characteristic of primary myelofibrosis. WHO diagnostic criteria of Essential thrombocytosis Major criteria Platelet count greater than or equal to 450,000/microliter.

Bone marrow biopsy Shows proliferation, mainly of the megakaryocytic lineage, with an increase in enlarged mature megakaryocytes. (Option A) No significant increase or left shift in neutrophil granulopoiesis or erythropoiesis is present, Very rarely a minor increase in reticulin fibers. (Option C) The presentation does not meet WHO criteria for BCR-ABL1 +ve CML, PCV, myelofibrosis, MDS, or other myeloid neoplasms.

Presence of JAK2, CALR, or MPL mutation. (Option B) Minor criteria: Presence of a clonal marker or absence of evidence of reactive thrombocytosis. Clinical features Thrombotic or hemorrhagic symptoms such as Bleeding tendency Microvascular occlusion Thrombosis of major arteries (leading to CVA and transient ischemic attacks), and vasomotor symptoms such as headache, visual disturbances, and syncope.
Mild splenomegaly and rarely hepatomegaly and lymphadenopathy

questions.question: A 65-year-old man presents with progressive fatigue and significant weight loss for the past six months. Examination reveals a markedly enlarged spleen. Peripheral blood smear shows teardrop-shaped red cells. Bone marrow biopsy confirms the diagnosis of primary myelofibrosis. Which of the following statements regarding the diagnosis is true? 1) It is characterized by extensive marrow fibrosis. 2) Diagnostic criteria include the presence of JAK2, CALR, or MPL mutations. 3) Pathogenesis involves the inappropriate release of fibrogenic factors like PDGF and TGF-β.

explanation.text: Primary myelofibrosis (PMF) is a chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by the development of extensive marrow fibrosis, which impairs normal hematopoiesis. (Statement 1) This fibrosis is driven by the inappropriate release of fibrogenic factors, such as platelet-derived growth factor and TGF-β, from neoplastic megakaryocytes. (Statement 3) Clinically, PMF presents with progressive anemia, splenomegaly, and symptoms like fatigue and weight loss.
WHO diagnostic criteria: Major criteria Megakaryocyte proliferation and atypia, usually with reticulin or collagen fibrosis.

Not meeting WHO criteria for BCR-ABL1 + CML, PV, ET, MDS, or other myeloid neoplasm Presence of JAK2, CALR, or MPL mutation or in the absence of these mutations, presence of other clonal markers or absence of minor reactive BM reticulin fibrosis. (Statement 2) Minor criteria: Leukocytosis ≥ 11 × 10 9 /L. Increased Serum Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH). Anemia not attributed to another condition. Palpable Splenomegaly.

questions.question: A 60-year-old man presents with complaints of increasing fatigue, early satiety, and unintentional weight loss over the past few months. On examination, there is palpable splenomegaly. Laboratory reports reveal pancytopenia with dacrocytes on the peripheral smear. Which of the following is not associated with Myelofibrosis?

explanation.text: Myeloblasts are seen in AML and are not associated with myelofibrosis. Myelofibrosis is the development of obliterative marrow fibrosis. Replacement of the marrow by fibrous tissue reduces bone marrow hematopoiesis, leading to cytopenias and extensive extramedullary hematopoiesis.

Investigations include CBC- pancytopenia due to obliterative bone marrow fibrosis Peripheral smear reveals a leukoerythroblastic blood picture where the distortion of the marrow leads to the premature release of immature erythroid and granulocyte (Option B) Teardrop-shaped red cells (dacrocytes) that are damaged during the birthing process in the fibrotic marrow (Option C) Bone marrow aspirate may reveal a dry tap. (Option A) May reveal thickening and distortion of bony trabeculae and deposition of reticulin and collagen fibers.

questions.question: A 75-year-old man presents with increasing fatigue, weakness, and easy bruising over the past few months. Labs show pancytopenia. Peripheral blood smear reveals dysplastic differentiation in the erythroid, granulocytic, monocytic, and megakaryocytic lineages. Which condition does this suggest?

explanation.text: Pawn ball megakaryocytes is associated with Myelodysplastic syndrome.

Myelodysplastic Syndrome (MDS) is a group of clonal stem cell disorders characterized by maturation defects and ineffective hematopoiesis with a risk transformation to AML Bone marrow replaced by clonal progeny of a neoplastic multipotent stem cell Leading to ineffective and disordered differentiation Can cause cytopenias and potential malignancy Genetic Causes Adults: Deletion of 5q chromosome Children: Monosomy 7 Types Primary (idiopathic) Secondary (due to genotoxic drugs or radiation therapy) Peripheral Smear Findings: Dysplastic differentiation of erythroid, granulocytic, monocytic, and megakaryocytic lineages Ring sideroblasts Erythroblasts with iron-laden mitochondria (visible as perinuclear granules in Prussian blue stain) Neutrophils with decreased secondary granules Döhle bodies PseudoPelger–Hüet cells (neutrophils with two nuclear lobes) Megakaryocytes with Single nuclear lobes Multiple separate nuclei (Pawnball megakaryocytes) Ringed sideroblasts: Döhle bodies: PseudoPelger–Hüet cells: Hyperlobated megakaryocytes (Option A): These are seen in Essential thrombocytosis, where peripheral smears reveal abnormally large platelets and marked thrombocytosis.
It is characterized by erythromelalgia, a throbbing and burning of hands and feet caused by the occlusion of small arterioles by platelet aggregates.

**Leukoerythroblastic picture (Option B):** This is seen in Myelofibrosis, which causes obliterative marrow fibrosis, decreasing hematopoiesis and causing cytopenias, with extensive extramedullary hematopoiesis.

**Increased proliferation of RBCs (Option C):** It is seen in Polycythemia Vera due to JAK2 mutation. Patients present with symptoms such as headaches, dizziness, and pruritus due to hyperviscosity. Bone marrow biopsy shows hypercellularity with increased erythropoiesis.

questions.question: A 5-year-old child presents with a skin rash, recurrent ear infections, bone pain, and polyuria. Imaging revealed lytic bone lesions and a biopsy of one of the lesions showed CD1a and S-100 positive Langerhans cells. Which of the following types of Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) is characterized by multifocal uni system involvement?

explanation.text: Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis (LCH) is a rare inflammatory and neoplastic condition that involves myeloid dendritic cells Genetic Mutation: BRAF V600E mutation found in the majority of cases BRAF gene encodes B-Raf, part of the MAPK pathway Mutation establishes the neoplastic nature of LCH Categories: Unisystem: Unifocal Multifocal Multisystem Types of langerhan histiocytosis: Eosinophilic granuloma (Option A) Hand-Schuller-Christian disease (Option B) Letterer-Siwe disease (Option C) Unifocal involvement.

Primarily involves lytic bone lesions. Seen in young children. Multifocal involvement. It is characterized by a triad of symptoms such as: Bony lesions in a calvarial defect. Diabetes insipidus and Exophthalmos. It is a more severe, disseminated form of LCH with multisystem involvement. It is characterized by lytic bony lesions and seborrheic dermatitis.

LCH Diagnosis: Light Microscopy Eosinophils appear as orange-looking cells Nuclei have a coffee bean appearance Immunohistochemistry (IHC): Positive markers: CD1a, CD207 (langerin), S100, HLA-DR Electron Microscopy:(Gold standard for diagnosis) Reveals tennis racket appearance of Birbeck granules
